verdict: OK to lend in Chakan auto components — pursue tier-2 EV-capable and tooling suppliers with tight monthly discipline; avoid single-OEM, ICE-engine-dependent, thin-margin converters.
title: Chakan Auto & Auto Components: a note to the credit manager
narrative: Pricing power is thin and passed through on commodity, so margin is a conversion fee. **So when a proposal lands, check the OEM approval letter and the commodity pass-through clause before anything else; if the buyer can unilaterally reset prices, ask for the last three price-revision notes.**

## What has changed now
**The India-wide signal is strong: IIP NIC 29 output +25.2% YoY and +19.2% Apr-to-date [D], with Maharashtra GST collections +8.6% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D].** But bank credit is running +27.0% YoY against output +19.2%, a +7.8 pp gap [D] — money is entering the chain faster than metal is moving. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the loan is funding real capacity or a working-capital stretch; if drawing power has grown faster than billed sales, ask why.** Locally, the only fresh news is Skoda VW transferring Chakan land to ARAI for a crash-test facility covering EV and ICE, Bharat NCAP and export testing [1][2][3] — a capability signal, not a demand number. **Sources say little about Chakan order books, so lean on first principles and peers here.**

## Where the growth is
**Peer results point to the same two lanes: EV-agnostic components and wiring/lightweighting.** Motherson Sumi Wiring grew revenue 46.7% to Rs 4,054 crore and net profit 35% to Rs 223 crore in Q2 [4]; ASK Automotive reported record revenue with aluminium squeezing margins and EV order wins in braking and lightweighting [5]; Lumax beat Q2 estimates and lifted its growth guide [7]. **So pursue tier-2 suppliers with EV or export order visibility and tooling capability; avoid pure ICE-engine-part converters, where obsolescence risk is explicit [11].**

## How to grow safely
**Structure on the working-capital cycle, not the P&L.** Gross current assets have averaged 160-170 days in recent years [10], so size limits to the actual cycle and take monthly stock-and-debtor statements, not quarterly. **Take every month: billed sales, debtor ageing by OEM, inventory days, and commodity hedge position — ICRA's analytical focus is on hedging policy and exposure relative to profits [8].** Cap debt/EBITDA at 2.5-2.75 times as a covenant [10], and require personal guarantee plus hypothecation of receivables. **If a borrower resists monthly data, treat that as the answer.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch debtor days by OEM first — a single-buyer concentration above half of sales is the structural risk in this cluster.** If one OEM stretches payment beyond the agreed cycle, cut limits before the next dispatch. If inventory days climb while billed sales flatten, the loan is funding unsold stock. If commodity hedging lapses, margin is exposed [8]. **Any of these three triggers a limit freeze and a fresh stock audit, not a conversation.**
watch: Top-buyer days stretch beyond agreed cycle -> freeze fresh limits and reprice
Inventory days rise while sales flatten -> cut drawing power and order stock audit
Hedge lapses or exposure exceeds profits -> require re-hedge before next disbursement
Crosses 2.5-2.75 times [10] -> stop new capex funding, restructure to working capital only
OEM order book / EV order wins (quarterly)
ICE-only order book shrinks -> shift exposure to EV-capable borrowers
